chapters.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current
chapters.summary: This chapter explores how electric currents create magnetic effects, building on prior knowledge of electricity and its heating effects. It introduces magnetic fields, electromagnetic effects, and electromagnets through hands-on activities such as observing compass needle deflection near a current-carrying wire.

book_skeleton.subject_overview: This textbook examines the relationship between electricity and magnetism, demonstrating how electric currents produce magnetic effects and vice versa. It covers magnetic fields, electromagnetic effects, and the operation of electromagnets through experimental activities.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_1:bar_magnet_field>> Sprinkle iron filings around a magnet, tap the table, and they leap into curving lines nobody drew. So who told them where to go? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The answer is that the magnet doesn't just sit there. It reaches out and changes the space all around itself, and we <<FOCUS:field-line-outer+field-line-mirror+field-line-far+field-line-mirror-far>> call that influenced region the magnetic field. <<SECTION:Magnetic Field|id=sec-1>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Magnetic field = region where a magnet can exert a force|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> A magnetic field is simply the region around a magnet where it can push or pull on something magnetic. Each iron filing feels that force and turns to line up with it. <<PAUSE:short>> Those lines the filings trace out have a name. <<TRACE:field-line-outer>> We call them magnetic field lines, and they are a map of the field, drawn so we can actually see something invisible. <<WRITE_TEXT:Field lines map the invisible field|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> But a line on its own only shows a shape. How do we know which way along the line the field actually points? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> We <<FOCUS:compass-body+compass-needle>> borrow a tiny compass. Put it on a line, and <<FOCUS:compass-needle>> its north tip swings to point along the field. <<UNFOCUS>> So the direction a compass north pole would move is the direction of the field line. <<WRITE_KEY:Outside the magnet, lines go N to S; they never cross|id=key-2>> Follow the arrows and you find a rule: outside the magnet, every field line <<FOCUS:north-pole>> leaves the north pole and <<FOCUS:field-line-outer-arrow+south-pole>> curves around into the south pole. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And here's a fact that catches people out: two field lines can never cross each other. <<WRITE_TEXT:Lines never cross|id=text-2>> <<PAUSE:short>> Why not? Because at any single point the compass can only point one way. If two lines crossed, the field would have two directions at once, and that is impossible. Notice too that the lines <<FOCUS:north-pole+south-pole>> bunch up tightly near the poles and spread apart in the middle. Where the lines crowd together, the field is strongest, which is exactly why the poles grab the iron filings hardest. <<WRITE_TEXT:Crowded lines = stronger field|id=text-3>> <<UNFOCUS>> So those curving filing patterns were never random. They are the magnet showing you its field, a real region of space where it can exert a force, mapped out by lines running north to south. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_1>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_1:current_wire_circuit>> Hold a compass under a perfectly ordinary copper wire, and nothing happens. Now switch on a current, and the needle swings sideways. Why sideways, and not toward the wire? <<PAUSE:long>> <<SECTION:Field around a straight wire|id=sec-1>> Let's build the experiment. Two or three small cells, a plug key, and a long straight copper wire, all joined in a single series loop. We lay that straight stretch of wire right over a tiny compass needle, and when we plug in the key, current begins to flow. The instant the current flows, the compass needle deflects. The wire that did nothing a moment ago is now behaving like a magnet. <<PAUSE:short>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_1:circular_field_around_wire>> So the moving charge makes a magnetic field. But the needle never points at the wire, <<FOCUS:compass-needle+straight-wire>> it sits across it. <<UNFOCUS>> That sideways twist is the clue to the field's true shape. <<WRITE_TEXT:Field lines are circles around the wire|id=text-1>> Picture <<FOCUS:straight-wire>> the wire running straight through the page. The field doesn't shoot outward like spokes, it <<FOCUS:field-circle-inner+field-circle-outer>> wraps around in closed circles. <<WRITE_KEY:A straight current-carrying wire is encircled by circular magnetic field lines|id=key-1>> These circles are concentric, <<FOCUS:straight-wire+field-circle-inner+field-circle-outer>> sharing the wire as their common centre, and a compass placed anywhere <<FOCUS:compass-needle>> lines up tangent to them, exactly the sideways twist we saw. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Notice the circles spread out as we move away. <<FOCUS:field-circle-inner>> Close to the wire they crowd together, meaning a strong field, and <<FOCUS:field-circle-outer>> farther out they thin, so the field grows weaker. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the test. If I reverse the cells so <<FOCUS:current-arrow>> the current runs the opposite way along the wire, what happens to that compass needle? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> The needle swings the other way entirely, from east right round to west. The whole <<FOCUS:field-inner-arrowhead+field-outer-arrowhead>> ring of arrows flips direction. <<WRITE_KEY:Reverse the current, reverse the field|id=key-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> That's the rule worth keeping. <<FOCUS:current-arrow>> Reverse the direction of the current, and you reverse <<FOCUS:field-inner-arrowhead+field-outer-arrowhead>> the direction of the magnetic field around it. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So a plain straight wire, once current flows, is sheathed in circles of magnetic field, stronger near the wire, and tied so tightly to the current that flipping one flips the other. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_2>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_2:wire_field_circles>> <<FOCUS:wire+current-arrow>> Current runs straight up this wire, yet the magnetic field it makes doesn't go straight at all. <<UNFOCUS>> Watch what it actually does. <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> If you stand a wire up through a piece of cardboard, sprinkle iron filings around it, and switch on the current, the filings snap into a pattern of rings, one inside another, all centred on the wire. <<SECTION:Field shape|id=sec-1>> <<WRITE_KEY:Field lines are concentric circles around the wire|id=key-1>> So here is the first big idea: the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire <<FOCUS:field-circle-inner+field-circle-outer>> forms concentric circles, not straight lines. <<PAUSE:short>> Notice the <<FOCUS:field-circle-outer>> circles get fainter as we move outward. The field is <<FOCUS:field-circle-inner>> strongest hugging the wire and weakens with distance, but every loop stays a closed circle. <<UNFOCUS>> These rings show the shape of the field, but a circle has two ways to go around. Clockwise or anticlockwise — which one is it? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:compass-needle>> Drop a tiny compass on one of the rings. Its <<FOCUS:compass-needle+field-circle-inner>> north pole always points along the circle, tangent to it, and that tells us the field has a definite direction of circulation. <<SECTION:The rule|id=sec-2>> <<UNFOCUS>> Here is the trick that makes it effortless. <<FOCUS:right-hand>> Take your right hand and imagine gripping the wire so your thumb points along the current. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Right thumb = current, curling fingers = field|id=key-2>> Your <<FOCUS:current-arrow>> thumb points up along the current, and your <<FOCUS:field-circle-inner>> curling fingers wrap around exactly the way the field circles the wire. <<UNFOCUS>> That is the right-hand thumb rule. <<PAUSE:short>> Let me line the hand up with our diagram. Thumb up along the current, fingers curling — and look, they <<FOCUS:right-hand+field-circle-inner+compass-needle>> follow the very same direction as our field circles and the compass needle. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's an example from the chapter. A current through a horizontal power line flows in the east to west direction. We want to find the direction of the magnetic field at a point directly below the wire and at a point directly above it. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Current in a horizontal power line flows east to west. Find the field direction directly below and directly above the wire.|id=ex-q-1>> We solve this by applying the right-hand thumb rule. We point the thumb of our right hand along the current, that is, from east to west, and the curl of our fingers gives the way the magnetic field wraps around the wire. <<WRITE_STEP:Point right thumb along current (east to west); fingers curl in the field direction.|id=ex-step-1-1>> Following the curl of the fingers, the field lies in a plane perpendicular to the wire. Viewed from the east end the field turns clockwise, and viewed from the west end it turns anti-clockwise. So at both points, above and below, the field circles the wire in this perpendicular plane. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The field circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire: clockwise when viewed from the east end, anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.|id=ex-ans-1>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Reverse current -> reverse field|id=text-1>>Now here is a neat check. If you flip the battery so current flows the other way, your thumb flips too, your fingers curl the opposite way, and <<FOCUS:field-circle-inner+field-circle-outer>> the whole field reverses. <<UNFOCUS>> So whenever someone asks which way the field points, you don't memorise it — you reach out your right hand, point your thumb along the current, and read the answer straight off your fingers. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_3:loop_field_lines>> You already know a straight wire wraps itself in neat circles of magnetic field. So what happens if you take that very wire and <<FOCUS:loop-wire>> bend it into a loop? <<PAUSE:long>> <<UNFOCUS>> Let's not throw away anything we know. The one rule that matters is this: the field around a straight wire gets weaker the farther out you go, so the circles drawn around it grow bigger and bigger with distance. <<SECTION:Bending the wire into a loop|id=sec-1>> Now look at any tiny piece of this curved wire. It doesn't care that the wire is bent. It still produces those same <<FOCUS:near-circles>> concentric circles of field hugging right up against it. <<UNFOCUS>> Near the wire the circles are small and tightly curved. But follow them as they <<TRACE:spreading-circles>> spread inward toward the middle of the loop, and watch them grow larger and larger. <<UNFOCUS>> Here's the question that makes a loop special: by the time these enormous circles reach the very centre, what does a tiny arc of such a giant circle actually look like? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> It looks like a straight line. Think of standing on the Earth: it's a giant sphere, but the patch of ground under your feet looks flat. <<WRITE_KEY:Big circles flatten into near-straight lines at the loop's centre|id=key-1>> In the same way, the big arcs flatten into <<FOCUS:centre-region>> near-straight lines right at the centre of the loop. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> And it's not just one piece of wire doing this. Every single section all the way around the loop sends its field through that centre as a straight line. Now apply the right-hand thumb rule to each section in turn. Curl your fingers in the direction of the current, and your <<FOCUS:current-arrow>> thumb points the way the field threads through the loop. <<UNFOCUS>> Do that for every part of the wire and you get the same answer every time: each section pushes the field through the centre in the very same direction. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Each part of loop adds same direction at centre|id=text-1>> So at the centre, the contributions don't cancel or fight each other. They all line up and add together into <<FOCUS:centre-field-arrow>> one bold, straight magnetic field shooting straight through the middle of the loop. <<PAUSE:short>> And because the whole loop is teaming up at that one spot, the field at the centre of a single loop is far stronger than the field around a plain straight wire carrying the same current. <<UNFOCUS>> So remember the two pictures: the giant circles flattening into straight lines at the centre, and every section of the loop pushing the field the same way so they pile up into one strong field through the middle. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_4>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_2_4:solenoid_field>> A plain piece of copper wire has no magnetism in it at all, yet wind it into a tight coil, switch on a current, and suddenly it pushes and pulls exactly like a bar magnet. <<SECTION:The Solenoid|id=sec-1>> This tightly wound coil, turn after turn packed close together in the shape of a cylinder, has a name: <<FOCUS:coil>> we call it a solenoid. <<UNFOCUS>> You already know a single loop of current makes a little magnetic field. So here is the honest question: what happens when you stack hundreds of those loops right next to each other? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> Inside the coil, <<FOCUS:internal-field-lines+internal-field-2+internal-field-3>> every loop pushes its field in the same direction, so they all add up. Watch them line up into <<TRACE:internal-field-lines>> straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines running straight down the middle. <<WRITE_KEY:Inside a solenoid the field is uniform and strong|id=key-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Because those inside lines are parallel and equally spaced everywhere, the magnetic field inside is the same at every point. We say the field inside is uniform, and it is strong. <<PAUSE:short>> Now follow the lines <<TRACE:external-field-lines>> out of the ends. They curl around the outside and loop all the way back, tracing the same graceful shape on the outside of the coil. <<WRITE_TEXT:Solenoid field = bar magnet field|id=text-1>> <<UNFOCUS>> Put this picture next to the field around an ordinary bar magnet and you will see they are remarkably similar. That is no coincidence. <<PAUSE:short>> The end where the lines stream out <<FOCUS:north-pole>> behaves as a north pole. <<PAUSE:short>> And the end where they dive back in <<FOCUS:south-pole>> behaves as a south pole. <<UNFOCUS>> A coil of wire has quietly become a magnet, with a north and a south, just from a flowing current. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Solenoid acts like a bar magnet: N at one end, S at the other|id=key-2>> So the magnet did not come from the copper. <<FOCUS:current-label>> It came from the current, shaped by the coil into the same field pattern as a bar magnet, with one end north and the other south. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Soft iron inside -> electromagnet|id=text-2>>And here is the payoff for the real world: slide a piece of soft iron into that strong, uniform field, and the field magnetises it. You have just built an electromagnet, the heart of motors, doorbells, and cranes that lift cars.

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_3>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_3:wire_in_field>> A wire just sits there, doing nothing. But run a current through it, put a magnet beside it, and the wire suddenly jumps. What pushed it? <<PAUSE:long>> Let's rewind to something you already know. When current flows through a wire, the wire wraps itself in a magnetic field, and that field can push or pull a nearby magnet. Now here comes a piece of beautiful reasoning from the French scientist Andre Marie Ampere. He said: if the current can push the magnet, then by simple fairness, the magnet must push back on the wire. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:Force on a current|id=sec-1>> So a magnet exerts a force on any wire that carries current. That single sentence is the heart of this whole idea. <<PAUSE:short>> Picture it for real. Here is a <<FOCUS:rod>> small aluminium rod, hung horizontally so it can swing freely, sitting right between the two poles of a strong <<FOCUS:north-pole+south-pole>> horse-shoe magnet. <<WRITE_TEXT:Field B points upward, current along rod|id=text-1>> The poles are arranged so the magnetic <<FOCUS:field-arrow>> field between them points straight up, and the <<FOCUS:current-arrow>> current runs along the rod from A to B. So we have two directions on the stage: the current going one way, <<FOCUS:field-arrow>> the field going another. <<UNFOCUS>> The big question is, which way does the rod actually move? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> The rod doesn't move along the current, and it doesn't move along the field. It gets <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> shoved sideways, perpendicular to both at once. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Force is perpendicular to both current and field|id=key-1>> That's the rule worth carving into memory: the <<FOCUS:force-arrow+current-arrow+field-arrow>> force is at right angles to both the current and the magnetic field, all three pointing in mutually perpendicular directions. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> Now watch what happens if we play with the directions. <<FOCUS:current-arrow>> Reverse the current, sending it from B back to A, and the rod gets pushed the opposite way. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Flip current OR field, and the force flips|id=key-2>> <<FOCUS:field-arrow>> Flip the magnet instead, so the field points down, and again the force reverses. <<UNFOCUS>> Change either one, and the push turns around. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. An electron enters a magnetic field at right angles to it, and we're asked: in which direction is the force acting on the electron? The choices are to the right, to the left, out of the page, or into the page. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Electron enters a magnetic field at right angles. Find the direction of the force on it.|id=ex-q-1>> We solve this using Fleming's left-hand rule, which tells us that the force is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the current. But there's a catch we must handle first. <<WRITE_STEP:Force is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the current (Fleming's left-hand rule)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Here's the key point to remember: the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of the electrons. So the current points the other way to the moving electron. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Current direction is taken opposite to the electron's motion|id=ex-step-1-2>> Applying Fleming's left-hand rule with the correct current direction, the force comes out directed into the page. So the answer is option (d), the force is directed into the page. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Answer: (d) Force is directed into the page|id=ex-ans-1>> And here is a lovely detail: the push is strongest when the current and the field are at right angles to each other, exactly as we set them up here. So the lesson is simple and powerful. A magnet shoves a current-carrying wire, the shove is sideways to both current and field, and flipping either one flips the shove. That single idea is what makes every electric motor on Earth spin. <<PAUSE:short>>

<<TOPIC_START:topic:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_4>>
<<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_4:home_three_wire_supply>> When your refrigerator's metal body develops a hidden electrical fault, why doesn't it kill the next person who touches it? <<PAUSE:long>> The answer is a clever three-wire system hiding inside every wall of your home, so let's follow the electricity in. <<SECTION:The two supply wires|id=sec-1>> Power arrives from the mains on two wires: <<FOCUS:live-wire>> the red live wire, which carries the supply, and <<FOCUS:neutral-wire>> the black neutral wire, which is the return path. <<UNFOCUS>> Between these two wires sits an electrical pressure of two hundred twenty volts, delivered as alternating current that flips back and forth fifty times every second. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Live + neutral = 220 V supply|id=text-1>> Every appliance is wired across these same two wires, side by side, which means they're all <<FOCUS:parallel-branch+appliance-lamp>> connected in parallel. <<UNFOCUS>> Connecting them in parallel means each appliance gets the full two hundred twenty volts and can be switched on or off without disturbing the others. <<SECTION:The fuse: a deliberate weak link|id=sec-2>> But what stops a sudden surge of current from melting your wiring and starting a fire? <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Fuse melts and breaks the circuit if current gets too high|id=key-1>> A fuse is a <<FOCUS:main-fuse>> thin wire placed on the live line that melts the instant the current climbs too high, breaking the circuit before anything dangerous happens. <<PAUSE:short>> <<SECTION:The earth wire: the lifesaver|id=sec-3>> Now back to that faulty refrigerator, and the third wire: <<FOCUS:earth-wire+appliance-body>> the green earth wire, connected to its metal body. The earth wire runs from the metal body straight down to <<FOCUS:earth-plate>> a metal plate buried deep in the ground near your house. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_KEY:Earth wire = low-resistance path to ground, keeps metal body safe|id=key-2>> If live electricity ever leaks onto the metal body, the earth wire offers a low-resistance path, so the current <<TRACE:earth-wire>> rushes harmlessly into the ground instead of through you. <<PAUSE:short>> And that surge of leaked current is large, so it also <<FOCUS:main-fuse>> blows the fuse, cutting the supply completely and double-protecting whoever touches the appliance next. <<PAUSE:short>> <<UNFOCUS>> So three wires do three jobs: live and neutral deliver the power in parallel, the fuse breaks a dangerous surge, and the earth wire quietly stands guard against a fatal shock.

lecture_plan.chapter_arc: We start with the surprising discovery that electricity and magnetism are two sides of the same coin — a current can deflect a compass needle. From there we build up the geometry of magnetic fields around wires, loops, and solenoids, then flip the relationship to see how a magnet pushes back on a current, and finally land in the home where these principles keep us safe.
lecture_plan.opening_hook: A compass needle sitting quietly near a wire suddenly twitches the moment you switch on the current — no magnet in sight. What invisible thing did the electricity just create, and how can we tame it to build motors, electromagnets, and the wiring in your walls?

coverage_checklist.description: Establish that a magnetic field is real and directional using field lines and compass behavior, including that field lines never cross and run N to S outside a magnet
Show experimentally that a current-carrying straight wire produces concentric circular magnetic field lines that weaken with distance and strengthen with current
Give a reliable way to predict field direction from current direction using the right-hand thumb rule
Trace how bending the wire into a loop and then a solenoid concentrates the field into a uniform bar-magnet-like field, motivating the electromagnet
Reverse the logic: a magnetic field exerts a force on a current-carrying conductor, and show the direction via Fleming's left-hand rule (basis of the motor)
Connect the chapter to real life — domestic wiring, live/neutral/earth wires, fuses, and electrical safety

lecture_plan.closing_summary: We opened with a compass needle twitching beside a wire — and now you know exactly why. A current always wraps an invisible magnetic field around itself, and the right-hand thumb rule tells you which way it points. Bend that wire into loops and a solenoid, and the field concentrates into something as strong and orderly as a bar magnet — the electromagnet. Flip the relationship and a magnet pushes back on a current, giving us the electric motor. And all of this isn't abstract: it's the same physics humming through the live, neutral, and earth wires that bring power safely into your home. From a single twitching needle to the wiring in your walls — that's the magnetic effect of electric current.

lesson_plans.title: Magnetic Field and Field Lines

hook.text: Sprinkle iron filings around a magnet, tap the table, and they leap into curving lines nobody drew. Who told them where to go?

crucial_facts: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet where it can exert a force; field lines point the way a compass north pole would move.
Field lines run from the north pole around to the south pole outside the magnet, and they never cross.

diagrams.purpose: Show the curving field-line pattern of a bar magnet so the field's shape and direction become visible.

required_elements.description: The north pole end of a horizontal bar magnet, marked N.
The south pole end of the bar magnet, marked S.
A representative curving field line arcing from the north pole around to the south pole outside the magnet, with an arrowhead showing direction.
A small compass needle placed on a field line, its red north tip aligned tangent to the line.

choreography.narration: Sprinkle iron filings around a magnet, tap the table, and they leap into curving lines nobody drew. So who told them where to go?

The answer is that the magnet doesn't just sit there. It reaches out and changes the space all around itself, and we call that influenced region the magnetic field. <<SECTION:Magnetic Field|id=sec-1>>

<<WRITE_KEY:Magnetic field = region where a magnet can exert a force|id=key-1>>A magnetic field is simply the region around a magnet where it can push or pull on something magnetic. Each iron filing feels that force and turns to line up with it.

Those lines the filings trace out have a name. We call them magnetic field lines, and they are a map of the field, drawn so we can actually see something invisible. <<WRITE_TEXT:Field lines map the invisible field|id=text-1>>
But a line on its own only shows a shape. How do we know which way along the line the field actually points?
We borrow a tiny compass. Put it on a line, and its north tip swings to point along the field. So the direction a compass north pole would move is the direction of the field line.

<<WRITE_KEY:Outside the magnet, lines go N to S; they never cross|id=key-2>>Follow the arrows and you find a rule: outside the magnet, every field line leaves the north pole and curves around into the south pole.
And here's a fact that catches people out: two field lines can never cross each other. <<WRITE_TEXT:Lines never cross|id=text-2>>
Why not? Because at any single point the compass can only point one way. If two lines crossed, the field would have two directions at once, and that is impossible.

Notice too that the lines bunch up tightly near the poles and spread apart in the middle. Where the lines crowd together, the field is strongest, which is exactly why the poles grab the iron filings hardest. <<WRITE_TEXT:Crowded lines = stronger field|id=text-3>>
So those curving filing patterns were never random. They are the magnet showing you its field, a real region of space where it can exert a force, mapped out by lines running north to south.

lesson_plans.title: Magnetic Field due to a Current through a Straight Conductor

hook.text: Hold a compass under a perfectly ordinary copper wire. Nothing happens. Now switch on a current… and the needle swings sideways. Why sideways, and not toward the wire?

crucial_facts: A current-carrying straight wire is wrapped in circular magnetic field lines that encircle it.
Reversing the direction of the current reverses the direction of the magnetic field.

diagrams.purpose: Show the simple series circuit that drives current through a straight wire laid over a compass, so the student sees exactly what produces the field.

required_elements.description: cells driving the current
the straight conductor section laid over the compass
the flowing current whose direction we will reverse

diagrams.purpose: Show that the magnetic field lines form concentric circles around the straight wire, and how their direction flips when the current reverses.

required_elements.description: a vertical straight wire seen end-on / along its length carrying current
an arrow along the wire showing the direction of conventional current

choreography.narration: Hold a compass under a perfectly ordinary copper wire, and nothing happens. Now switch on a current, and the needle swings sideways. Why sideways, and not toward the wire?
<<SECTION:Field around a straight wire|id=sec-1>>Let's build the experiment. Two or three small cells, a plug key, and a long straight copper wire, all joined in a single series loop.
We lay that straight stretch of wire right over a tiny compass needle, and when we plug in the key, current begins to flow.
The instant the current flows, the compass needle deflects. The wire that did nothing a moment ago is now behaving like a magnet.
So the moving charge makes a magnetic field. But the needle never points at the wire, it sits across it. That sideways twist is the clue to the field's true shape.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Field lines are circles around the wire|id=text-1>>Picture the wire running straight through the page. The field doesn't shoot outward like spokes, it wraps around in closed circles.

<<WRITE_KEY:A straight current-carrying wire is encircled by circular magnetic field lines|id=key-1>>These circles are concentric, sharing the wire as their common centre, and a compass placed anywhere lines up tangent to them, exactly the sideways twist we saw.
Notice the circles spread out as we move away. Close to the wire they crowd together, meaning a strong field, and farther out they thin, so the field grows weaker.
Here's the test. If I reverse the cells so the current runs the opposite way along the wire, what happens to that compass needle?
The needle swings the other way entirely, from east right round to west. The whole ring of arrows flips direction.
<<WRITE_KEY:Reverse the current, reverse the field|id=key-2>>That's the rule worth keeping. Reverse the direction of the current, and you reverse the direction of the magnetic field around it.
So a plain straight wire, once current flows, is sheathed in circles of magnetic field, stronger near the wire, and tied so tightly to the current that flipping one flips the other.

lesson_plans.title: The Right-Hand Thumb Rule

hook.text: Current runs straight up a wire — so why does its magnetic field bend into perfect circles around it instead of shooting off in a straight line?

crucial_facts: The magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire forms concentric circles, not straight lines.
Point your right thumb along the current, and your curling fingers show the direction the field circles around the wire.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the magnetic field around a straight wire is a set of concentric circles, and let the student read off the field direction with the right-hand thumb rule.

required_elements.description: A straight vertical wire passing through the centre, carrying current upward.
An upward arrow along the wire showing conventional current direction.
An inner concentric circle around the wire representing a magnetic field line, with a small arrowhead showing its circulation direction.
An outer concentric circle around the wire, weaker, also with an arrowhead showing circulation direction.
A small compass needle placed on the inner circle at point P, its north pole tangent to the circle showing field direction.
A right hand with thumb pointing up along the wire and fingers curling around it in the direction of the field circles.

choreography.narration: Current runs straight up this wire, yet the magnetic field it makes doesn't go straight at all. Watch what it actually does.
If you stand a wire up through a piece of cardboard, sprinkle iron filings around it, and switch on the current, the filings snap into a pattern of rings, one inside another, all centred on the wire.

<<SECTION:Field shape|id=sec-1>><<WRITE_KEY:Field lines are concentric circles around the wire|id=key-1>>So here is the first big idea: the magnetic field around a straight current-carrying wire forms concentric circles, not straight lines.
Notice the circles get fainter as we move outward. The field is strongest hugging the wire and weakens with distance, but every loop stays a closed circle.
These rings show the shape of the field, but a circle has two ways to go around. Clockwise or anticlockwise — which one is it?
Drop a tiny compass on one of the rings. Its north pole always points along the circle, tangent to it, and that tells us the field has a definite direction of circulation.
<<SECTION:The rule|id=sec-2>>Here is the trick that makes it effortless. Take your right hand and imagine gripping the wire so your thumb points along the current.

<<WRITE_KEY:Right thumb = current, curling fingers = field|id=key-2>>Your thumb points up along the current, and your curling fingers wrap around exactly the way the field circles the wire. That is the right-hand thumb rule.
Let me line the hand up with our diagram. Thumb up along the current, fingers curling — and look, they follow the very same direction as our field circles and the compass needle.

Here's an example from the chapter. A current through a horizontal power line flows in the east to west direction. We want to find the direction of the magnetic field at a point directly below the wire and at a point directly above it. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Current in a horizontal power line flows east to west. Find the field direction directly below and directly above the wire.|id=ex-q-1>>

We solve this by applying the right-hand thumb rule. We point the thumb of our right hand along the current, that is, from east to west, and the curl of our fingers gives the way the magnetic field wraps around the wire. <<WRITE_STEP:Point right thumb along current (east to west); fingers curl in the field direction.|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Following the curl of the fingers, the field lies in a plane perpendicular to the wire. Viewed from the east end the field turns clockwise, and viewed from the west end it turns anti-clockwise. So at both points, above and below, the field circles the wire in this perpendicular plane. <<WRITE_ANSWER:The field circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire: clockwise when viewed from the east end, anti-clockwise when viewed from the west end.|id=ex-ans-1>>

<<WRITE_TEXT:Reverse current -> reverse field|id=text-1>>Now here is a neat check. If you flip the battery so current flows the other way, your thumb flips too, your fingers curl the opposite way, and the whole field reverses.
So whenever someone asks which way the field points, you don't memorise it — you reach out your right hand, point your thumb along the current, and read the answer straight off your fingers.

lesson_plans.title: Magnetic Field of a Current-Carrying Circular Loop

hook.text: You already know a straight wire wraps itself in circles of magnetic field. So what happens if you take that wire and bend it into a loop?

crucial_facts: At the centre of a current loop, the field lines from every part of the wire all point the same way, so they add up into one strong straight field through the middle.
The huge looping circles around the far side of the wire flatten into near-straight lines by the time they reach the centre of the loop.

diagrams.purpose: Show that the concentric circles around each section of the bent wire grow larger moving inward and appear straight and aligned at the loop centre.

required_elements.description: A current-carrying wire bent into a vertical circular loop, drawn side-on as an ellipse, with a small current-direction arrow on it.
Small tightly-curved concentric circles of magnetic field hugging the wire near the top and bottom sections of the loop.
Larger concentric field circles that grow bigger as they spread inward from the wire toward the loop's interior.
The central region inside the loop where the arcs of the big circles appear as straight lines.
A bold straight arrow through the centre of the loop showing the net magnetic field, perpendicular to the plane of the loop.

choreography.narration: You already know a straight wire wraps itself in neat circles of magnetic field. So what happens if you take that very wire and bend it into a loop?

Let's not throw away anything we know. The one rule that matters is this: the field around a straight wire gets weaker the farther out you go, so the circles drawn around it grow bigger and bigger with distance.

<<SECTION:Bending the wire into a loop|id=sec-1>>Now look at any tiny piece of this curved wire. It doesn't care that the wire is bent. It still produces those same concentric circles of field hugging right up against it.
Near the wire the circles are small and tightly curved. But follow them as they spread inward toward the middle of the loop, and watch them grow larger and larger.
Here's the question that makes a loop special: by the time these enormous circles reach the very centre, what does a tiny arc of such a giant circle actually look like?

It looks like a straight line. Think of standing on the Earth: it's a giant sphere, but the patch of ground under your feet looks flat. <<WRITE_KEY:Big circles flatten into near-straight lines at the loop's centre|id=key-1>>In the same way, the big arcs flatten into near-straight lines right at the centre of the loop.
And it's not just one piece of wire doing this. Every single section all the way around the loop sends its field through that centre as a straight line.
Now apply the right-hand thumb rule to each section in turn. Curl your fingers in the direction of the current, and your thumb points the way the field threads through the loop.
Do that for every part of the wire and you get the same answer every time: each section pushes the field through the centre in the very same direction.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Each part of loop adds same direction at centre|id=text-1>>So at the centre, the contributions don't cancel or fight each other. They all line up and add together into one bold, straight magnetic field shooting straight through the middle of the loop.
And because the whole loop is teaming up at that one spot, the field at the centre of a single loop is far stronger than the field around a plain straight wire carrying the same current.

So remember the two pictures: the giant circles flattening into straight lines at the centre, and every section of the loop pushing the field the same way so they pile up into one strong field through the middle.

lesson_plans.title: The Solenoid: Building a Magnet from a Coil of Wire

hook.text: A plain piece of copper wire has no magnetism in it at all. Yet wind it into a coil, switch on a current, and you get something that pushes and pulls exactly like a bar magnet. Where did that magnet come from?

crucial_facts: A current-carrying solenoid produces a magnetic field identical in pattern to a bar magnet, with one end acting as a north pole and the other as a south pole.
Inside the solenoid the field lines are parallel and evenly spaced, which means the magnetic field there is uniform and strong.

choreography.narration: A plain piece of copper wire has no magnetism in it at all, yet wind it into a tight coil, switch on a current, and suddenly it pushes and pulls exactly like a bar magnet.
<<SECTION:The Solenoid|id=sec-1>>This tightly wound coil, turn after turn packed close together in the shape of a cylinder, has a name: we call it a solenoid.
You already know a single loop of current makes a little magnetic field. So here is the honest question: what happens when you stack hundreds of those loops right next to each other?
Inside the coil, every loop pushes its field in the same direction, so they all add up. Watch them line up into straight, parallel, evenly spaced lines running straight down the middle.

<<WRITE_KEY:Inside a solenoid the field is uniform and strong|id=key-1>>Because those inside lines are parallel and equally spaced everywhere, the magnetic field inside is the same at every point. We say the field inside is uniform, and it is strong.
Now follow the lines out of the ends. They curl around the outside and loop all the way back, tracing the same graceful shape on the outside of the coil.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Solenoid field = bar magnet field|id=text-1>>Put this picture next to the field around an ordinary bar magnet and you will see they are remarkably similar. That is no coincidence.
The end where the lines stream out behaves as a north pole.
And the end where they dive back in behaves as a south pole. A coil of wire has quietly become a magnet, with a north and a south, just from a flowing current.

<<WRITE_KEY:Solenoid acts like a bar magnet: N at one end, S at the other|id=key-2>>So the magnet did not come from the copper. It came from the current, shaped by the coil into the same field pattern as a bar magnet, with one end north and the other south.

<<WRITE_TEXT:Soft iron inside -> electromagnet|id=text-2>>And here is the payoff for the real world: slide a piece of soft iron into that strong, uniform field, and the field magnetises it. You have just built an electromagnet, the heart of motors, doorbells, and cranes that lift cars.

<<WRITE_KEY:Flip current OR field, and the force flips|id=key-2>>Flip the magnet instead, so the field points down, and again the force reverses. Change either one, and the push turns around.

We solve this using Fleming's left-hand rule, which tells us that the force is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the current. But there's a catch we must handle first. <<WRITE_STEP:Force is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the current (Fleming's left-hand rule)|id=ex-step-1-1>>

Here's the key point to remember: the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of the electrons. So the current points the other way to the moving electron. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Current direction is taken opposite to the electron's motion|id=ex-step-1-2>>

Applying Fleming's left-hand rule with the correct current direction, the force comes out directed into the page. So the answer is option (d), the force is directed into the page. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Answer: (d) Force is directed into the page|id=ex-ans-1>>
And here is a lovely detail: the push is strongest when the current and the field are at right angles to each other, exactly as we set them up here.

lesson_plans.title: How Electricity Comes Home Safely

hook.text: When your refrigerator's metal body gets a hidden electrical fault, why doesn't it kill the next person who touches it?

crucial_facts: The earth wire gives leaked current a low-resistance path into the ground, so a faulty metal body stays safe to touch.
Live and neutral carry the 220-volt supply; the fuse breaks the circuit if the current gets dangerously high.

diagrams.purpose: Show the three wires entering a home and how live and neutral feed appliances in parallel, with the earth wire branching to a metal-bodied appliance and down to the ground.

required_elements.description: Red live wire entering the house from the mains, carrying the supply.

Green earth wire branching off to the metal body of an appliance.

choreography.narration: When your refrigerator's metal body develops a hidden electrical fault, why doesn't it kill the next person who touches it?
The answer is a clever three-wire system hiding inside every wall of your home, so let's follow the electricity in.
<<SECTION:The two supply wires|id=sec-1>>Power arrives from the mains on two wires: the red live wire, which carries the supply, and the black neutral wire, which is the return path.
Between these two wires sits an electrical pressure of two hundred twenty volts, delivered as alternating current that flips back and forth fifty times every second.
<<WRITE_TEXT:Live + neutral = 220 V supply|id=text-1>>Every appliance is wired across these same two wires, side by side, which means they're all connected in parallel.
Connecting them in parallel means each appliance gets the full two hundred twenty volts and can be switched on or off without disturbing the others.
<<SECTION:The fuse: a deliberate weak link|id=sec-2>>But what stops a sudden surge of current from melting your wiring and starting a fire?

<<WRITE_KEY:Fuse melts and breaks the circuit if current gets too high|id=key-1>>A fuse is a thin wire placed on the live line that melts the instant the current climbs too high, breaking the circuit before anything dangerous happens.
<<SECTION:The earth wire: the lifesaver|id=sec-3>>Now back to that faulty refrigerator, and the third wire: the green earth wire, connected to its metal body.
The earth wire runs from the metal body straight down to a metal plate buried deep in the ground near your house.

<<WRITE_KEY:Earth wire = low-resistance path to ground, keeps metal body safe|id=key-2>>If live electricity ever leaks onto the metal body, the earth wire offers a low-resistance path, so the current rushes harmlessly into the ground instead of through you.
And that surge of leaked current is large, so it also blows the fuse, cutting the supply completely and double-protecting whoever touches the appliance next.
So three wires do three jobs: live and neutral deliver the power in parallel, the fuse breaks a dangerous surge, and the earth wire quietly stands guard against a fatal shock.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's start with something you've probably played with: a compass needle. Here's a neat fact — a compass needle is actually a tiny bar magnet. Its two ends point roughly toward north and south. The end pointing north we call the north pole, or north-seeking pole, and the end pointing south we call the south pole. And the rule you may already know is that like poles push each other away, while unlike poles pull toward each other.

Now imagine placing a bar magnet on a sheet of paper and sprinkling iron filings all around it. When you tap the board gently, something beautiful happens — those tiny iron pieces line up in a curving pattern. Why? Because the magnet reaches out and influences the space around it. Each iron filing feels a force, and that force arranges them into neat lines. The whole region around the magnet where you can detect its force is called its magnetic field. And the lines the filings trace out are called magnetic field lines.

You can draw these lines yourself with a small compass. You place the compass near the north pole, mark where the needle points, then keep stepping along, marking points, until you reach the south pole. Join those points with a smooth curve, and you've drawn a field line.

Here's the important idea about direction. A magnetic field has both a direction and a strength — we call something with both of these a quantity with direction and magnitude. By convention, the direction of the field is the way a north pole of the compass would move. So the field lines come out of the north pole and go into the south pole on the outside of the magnet. But inside the magnet, the lines run from south pole back to north pole. That means each field line is actually a closed loop — a closed curve.

Notice something clever: where the field lines are crowded close together, the field is stronger, meaning it pushes or pulls harder there. Where they spread apart, the field is weaker. So the closeness of the lines is like a map of strength.

One last rule, and it's a logical one. No two field lines ever cross each other. Think about why. If two lines crossed at a point, the compass needle sitting there would have to point in two different directions at once — and that's simply impossible. A compass can only point one way. So field lines never intersect.

What happens to the deflection of the compass needle placed at a
given point if the current in the copper wire is changed? To see this, vary
the current in the wire. We find that the deflection in the needle also
changes. In fact, if the current is increased, the deflection also increases.

point increases as the current through the wire increases.

away from the copper wire but the current through the wire remains the
same? To see this, now place the compass at a farther point from the
conducting wire (say at point Q). What change do you observe? We see
that the deflection in the needle decreases. Thus the magnetic field

topics.our_understanding:
Let's explore what happens around a wire when electric current flows through it. We already know that a current-carrying wire behaves like a magnet, so now we want to figure out the pattern of that magnetism. To start, imagine taking a long straight copper wire, two or three cells of one point five volts each, and a plug key, all connected in a series circuit. You lay this straight wire parallel to and right above a small compass needle. When you plug in the key and let current flow, watch the compass needle. If the current is flowing from north to south, the north pole of the needle swings toward the east. That tells us a magnetic field has appeared around the wire, and the needle is lining up with it.

Now here's the clever part. Reverse the connections so the current flows the other way, from south to north. The needle now swings in the opposite direction, toward the west. This is a key insight: the direction of the magnetic field depends on the direction of the current. Flip the current, and you flip the field.

Next, let's ask about strength. Imagine a thicker setup with a twelve volt battery, a variable resistance called a rheostat, and an ammeter that reads up to five amperes, with a thick copper wire poked straight up through a piece of cardboard. If you change the current and watch a compass needle at a fixed spot, you'll notice the deflection changes too. When you increase the current, the deflection increases. This means the magnetic field at that point gets stronger as more current flows through the wire.

Then try something else. Keep the current the same, but move the compass farther away from the wire, say to a point we'll call Q. Now the deflection shrinks. So the magnetic field gets weaker as you move away from the wire. Think about the diagram we'll look at, where the magnetic field is drawn as a set of concentric circles around the wire. Those circles grow larger and more spread out the farther you go, which is a nice picture for why the field weakens with distance. So to sum up: a current makes a magnetic field, reversing the current reverses the field, more current means a stronger field, and greater distance means a weaker field.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's figure out something that often confuses people. When electric current flows through a straight wire, it creates a magnetic field around it. But which way does that field point? We need a reliable rule, and that's exactly what this section gives us.

First, imagine a simple experiment. You stand a copper wire straight up, passing through a piece of cardboard, and connect it to a battery so current flows. Then you sprinkle iron filings on the cardboard and gently tap it. What you'll see is beautiful: the filings line up in a pattern of circles, one inside the other, all centered on the wire. These concentric circles are the magnetic field lines. They tell us the field wraps around the wire in loops, not in straight lines.

Now, the circles show the shape of the field, but not its direction. To find direction, you place a small compass on one of the circles. The way the north pole of the compass needle points tells you which way the field lines go at that spot. And here's a neat thing to notice: if you reverse the current, by swapping the battery connections, the field lines reverse too. The direction of the field depends on the direction of the current.

So how do we remember the direction without always running an experiment? That's where the right-hand thumb rule comes in. Imagine grabbing the wire with your right hand so your thumb points in the direction the current is flowing. Then your curled fingers wrap around the wire, and the way they wrap shows you the direction of the magnetic field lines. That's it. Thumb for current, fingers for field.

This rule is also called Maxwell's corkscrew rule. Picture turning a corkscrew so it moves forward in the direction of the current. The way you twist your hand to drive it in tells you the direction of the magnetic field. Both pictures give the same answer.

Why does this matter? Because almost everything electrical, from doorbells to electric motors, depends on knowing how current and magnetic fields relate. Once you can predict the direction of the field just by pointing your thumb, you've unlocked a tool you'll use again and again. Try it right now with your own hand. Point your thumb up, and watch your fingers curl. That curl is the magnetic field.

topics.our_understanding:
So far you've pictured the magnetic field around a straight wire carrying current — those neat circles wrapping around the wire. Now let's bend that wire into a circle, a loop, and pass current through it. What happens to the field then?

Here's the key idea you already know: the magnetic field around a straight wire gets weaker as you move farther away from it. The circles representing the field grow bigger and bigger the farther out you go. Now imagine taking that wire and curling it into a loop. At every single point along that curved wire, there are still these concentric circles of magnetic field. Near the wire they're small and tightly curved, but as they spread out toward the center of the loop, they grow so large that, by the time they reach the very center, the arcs look almost like straight lines.

So here's the beautiful result. Every little piece of the looped wire sends its magnetic field through the center, and if you apply the right-hand rule to each piece, you find they all point in the same direction inside the loop. That means all those contributions add together and reinforce each other. The field at the center of the loop comes out strong and pointing straight through, perpendicular to the plane of the loop.

Now think about making it even stronger. The field from a current-carrying wire depends directly on the current flowing through it — more current, more field. But there's a clever trick. Instead of one loop, wind the wire into a coil with many turns. Suppose you have a coil with a certain number of turns, let's call it n turns. Because the current in each turn flows in the same direction, the field from each turn adds onto the others. So a coil with n turns produces a field that is n times as large as a single loop would. Notice how powerful that is — by simply winding more loops, you multiply the strength without needing more current.

This is exactly why electromagnets and many electrical devices use coils with many tightly wound turns. To see it for yourself, you can sprinkle iron filings on a cardboard with a multi-turn coil poking through it, send current through, tap gently, and watch the filings line up to reveal the field pattern. The physics on paper becomes something you can actually see with your own eyes.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about a really useful device called a solenoid. Imagine you take a long piece of insulated copper wire and wind it round and round, turn after turn, packing the loops close together so they form the shape of a cylinder. That tightly wound coil is what we call a solenoid. Now here's the exciting part: when you pass an electric current through it, something special happens to the space around and inside it.

Think about the magnetic field that forms. If you look at the pattern of the field lines around a current-carrying solenoid, and then compare it with the field lines around an ordinary bar magnet, you'll notice they look remarkably similar. That's not a coincidence. One end of the solenoid actually behaves like a magnetic north pole, and the other end behaves like a south pole. So a coil carrying current is acting just like a bar magnet, which is pretty amazing when you stop to think about it.

Now pay close attention to what happens inside the solenoid. The field lines in there are parallel straight lines, all running in the same direction, evenly spaced. What does that tell us? It tells us the magnetic field has the same strength and the same direction at every point inside the coil. When a field is the same at all points like this, we call it a uniform magnetic field. This idea of uniformity is really important, because a uniform field is steady and predictable, and that makes it very handy in real applications.

Here's where it gets practical. The magnetic field inside a solenoid can be made quite strong. So if you place a piece of magnetic material, like a rod of soft iron, inside the coil while the current flows, that strong field will magnetise the iron. The iron itself becomes a magnet. A magnet made this way, by using the magnetic effect of a current flowing through a solenoid, is called an electromagnet. The clever thing about an electromagnet is that you can switch it on and off just by switching the current on and off. That control is why electromagnets show up in so many devices around us. So remember the key chain of ideas here: tightly wound coil, current flowing, magnetic field like a bar magnet, uniform field inside, and a way to make a strong, controllable magnet.

topics.our_understanding:
Let's build on something we already know. When electric current flows through a wire, it creates a magnetic field around it, and that field can push or pull on a nearby magnet. Now here's a beautiful piece of reasoning from the French scientist Andre Marie Ampere. He said: if the current can push the magnet, then by fairness, the magnet must push back on the current-carrying wire with an equal and opposite force. So a magnet exerts a force on a wire that carries current. That's the big idea of this section.

To see this for yourself, imagine hanging a small aluminium rod horizontally so it can swing freely. Place a strong horse-shoe magnet around it so the rod sits between the two poles, with the magnetic field pointing upward. Now connect the rod to a battery so current flows through it. What happens? The rod jumps sideways. It gets pushed in one direction. And here's the clever part: if you reverse the current, the rod jumps the other way. If instead you flip the magnet so the field points downward, the rod again moves the opposite way. So the direction of the force depends on two things: the direction of the current, and the direction of the magnetic field.

Notice something important. The push is strongest when the current and the magnetic field are at right angles to each other, ninety degrees apart. And the force itself points in a third direction, perpendicular to both the current and the field. So we have three directions all at right angles, like the corners of a room.

To keep track of these three directions, we use a handy trick called Fleming's left-hand rule. Stretch out the thumb, the forefinger, and the middle finger of your left hand so they all point at right angles to each other. Point your first finger in the direction of the magnetic field. Point your second finger in the direction of the current. Then your thumb shows you the direction of the force, the way the conductor moves.

Why does this matter? Because this single idea powers an amazing list of devices around you: electric motors, electric generators, loudspeakers, microphones, and measuring instruments all rely on the force a magnetic field exerts on a current. Master this rule, and you understand the heartbeat of a huge part of our technology.

topics.standalone_narration_text: <<FOCUS:rod>> <<SHOW_DIAGRAM:diagram:physics:magnetic_effects_of_electric_current:12_3:wire_in_field>> A wire just sits there, doing nothing. But run a current through it, put a magnet beside it, and the wire suddenly jumps. What pushed it? <<PAUSE:long>> Let's rewind to something you already know. When current flows through a wire, the wire wraps itself in a magnetic field, and that field can push or pull a nearby magnet. <<POINT:current-arrow>> <<FOCUS:north-pole>> Now here comes a piece of beautiful reasoning from the French scientist Andre Marie Ampere. He said: if the current can push the magnet, then by simple fairness, the magnet must push back on the wire. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:south-pole>> <<SECTION:Force on a current|id=sec-1>>So a magnet exerts a force on any wire that carries current. That single sentence is the heart of this whole idea. <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:rod>> Picture it for real. Here is a small aluminium rod, hung horizontally so it can swing freely, sitting right between the two poles of a strong horse-shoe magnet. <<FOCUS:field-arrow>> <<WRITE_TEXT:Field B points upward, current along rod|id=text-1>>The poles are arranged so the magnetic field between them points straight up, and the current runs along the rod from A to B. <<POINT:field-arrow>> So we have two directions on the stage: the current going one way, the field going another. The big question is, which way does the rod actually move? <<POINT:current-arrow>> <<PAUSE:long>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> The rod doesn't move along the current, and it doesn't move along the field. It gets shoved sideways, perpendicular to both at once. <<TRACE:force-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Force is perpendicular to both current and field|id=key-1>>That's the rule worth carving into memory: the force is at right angles to both the current and the magnetic field, all three pointing in mutually perpendicular directions. <<PAUSE:short>> Now watch what happens if we play with the directions. Reverse the current, sending it from B back to A, and the rod gets pushed the opposite way. <<POINT:current-arrow>> <<PAUSE:short>> <<FOCUS:field-arrow>> <<WRITE_KEY:Flip current OR field, and the force flips|id=key-2>>Flip the magnet instead, so the field points down, and again the force reverses. Change either one, and the push turns around. <<PAUSE:short>> Here's an example from the chapter. An electron enters a magnetic field at right angles to it, and we're asked: in which direction is the force acting on the electron? The choices are to the right, to the left, out of the page, or into the page. <<WRITE_TEXT:Q: Electron enters a magnetic field at right angles. Find the direction of the force on it.|id=ex-q-1>> We solve this using Fleming's left-hand rule, which tells us that the force is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the current. But there's a catch we must handle first. <<WRITE_STEP:Force is perpendicular to both the magnetic field and the current (Fleming's left-hand rule)|id=ex-step-1-1>> Here's the key point to remember: the direction of current is taken opposite to the direction of motion of the electrons. So the current points the other way to the moving electron. <<PAUSE:short>> <<WRITE_STEP:Current direction is taken opposite to the electron's motion|id=ex-step-1-2>> Applying Fleming's left-hand rule with the correct current direction, the force comes out directed into the page. So the answer is option (d), the force is directed into the page. <<WRITE_ANSWER:Answer: (d) Force is directed into the page|id=ex-ans-1>> <<FOCUS:rod>> And here is a lovely detail: the push is strongest when the current and the field are at right angles to each other, exactly as we set them up here. <<FOCUS:force-arrow>> So the lesson is simple and powerful. A magnet shoves a current-carrying wire, the shove is sideways to both current and field, and flipping either one flips the shove. That single idea is what makes every electric motor on Earth spin. <<PAUSE:short>>

In our homes, we receive supply of electric power through a main supply
(also called mains), either supported through overhead electric poles or
by underground cables. One of the wires in this supply, usually with
red insulation cover, is called live wire (or positive). Another wire, with
black insulation, is called neutral wire (or negative). In our country, the
potential difference between the two is 220 V.
At the meter-board in the house, these wires pass into an electricity
meter through a main fuse. Through the main switch they are connected
to the line wires in the house. These wires supply electricity to separate
circuits within the house. Often, two separate circuits are used, one of
15 A current rating for appliances with higher power ratings such as
geysers, air coolers, etc. The other circuit is of 5 A current rating for
bulbs, fans, etc. The earth wire, which has insulation of green colour, is
usually connected to a metal plate deep in the earth near the house.
This is used as a safety measure, especially for those appliances that
have a metallic body, for example, electric press, toaster, table fan,
refrigerator, etc. The metallic body is connected to the earth wire, which
provides a low-resistance conducting path for the current. Thus, it
ensures that any leakage of current to the metallic body of the appliance
keeps its potential to that of the earth, and the user may not get a severe
electric shock.

Magnetism in medicine
An electric current always produces a magnetic field. Even weak ion currents that
travel along the nerve cells in our body produce magnetic fields. When we touch
something, our nerves carry an electric impulse to the muscles we need to use. This

topics.our_understanding:
Let's talk about how electricity actually comes into your home and keeps you safe. The power that reaches your house comes through what we call the mains, either through overhead poles or underground cables. There are two main wires here. One has red insulation and we call it the live wire, sometimes called positive. The other has black insulation and we call it the neutral wire, or negative. In our country, the difference in electrical pressure, or potential difference, between these two wires is two hundred twenty volts. This power comes in as AC, alternating current, with a frequency of fifty hertz.

Now, before this electricity spreads through your house, it passes through an electricity meter and a main fuse, and then a main switch. From there, the house usually splits into two separate circuits. One circuit has a current rating of fifteen amperes for the big, power-hungry appliances like geysers and air coolers. The other circuit has a five ampere rating for lighter things like bulbs and fans.

There's also a third wire, with green insulation, called the earth wire. This one is connected to a metal plate buried deep in the ground near your house. Why does this matter? Imagine an appliance with a metal body, like an electric iron, toaster, or refrigerator. If by accident some current leaks onto that metal body, and you touch it, you could get a nasty shock. The earth wire gives that leaking current an easy, low-resistance path straight into the ground, so the metal body stays at the same potential as the earth. That keeps you safe.

Notice how appliances are wired. Each one connects across the live and neutral wires, and each has its own switch. They're all connected in parallel, so every appliance gets the same potential difference of two hundred twenty volts.

Finally, the fuse is the real hero of safety. A fuse protects your circuit from overloading and short-circuiting. A short circuit happens when the live and neutral wires touch directly, maybe because the insulation got damaged. When that happens, the current shoots up suddenly and dangerously. The fuse is built so that this huge current heats it up through Joule heating until it melts, breaking the circuit before anything catches fire. Overloading can also happen if the supply voltage jumps too high, or if you plug too many appliances into one socket. So the fuse quietly watches over everything, ready to sacrifice itself to keep you and your appliances safe.

questions.q_text: A student wants to draw a single magnetic field line around a bar magnet using a small compass. Describe the step-by-step method they should follow and explain why the resulting curve represents a field line with a direction.
questions.answer: Step 1: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and mark its north and south poles. Step 2: Place the small compass near the north pole of the magnet. The compass needle will line up with the magnet's field. Step 3: Mark a dot on the paper at the position the north end of the compass needle points to. Step 4: Move the compass forward so that its tail sits on the dot you just made, and again mark where the north end now points. Step 5: Keep repeating this stepping-and-marking process, moving along until you reach the south pole of the magnet. Step 6: Join all the marked dots with a smooth curve. This curve is one magnetic field line. It has a direction because, by convention, the direction of a magnetic field is the way the north pole of the compass would move — so the line runs out of the north pole, around the outside, and into the south pole. The arrows along it point in that same direction the compass needle indicated at each step.

questions.q_text: A student observes a certain compass deflection at a point near a straight wire. She then doubles the current but also moves the compass much farther from the wire. Explain how each change affects the magnetic field at the compass, and why the final deflection cannot be predicted with certainty from the rules given.
questions.answer: Step 1: Consider the effect of increasing the current. From the experiments, when current increases the magnetic field at a fixed point gets stronger, so doubling the current acts to increase the deflection. Step 2: Consider the effect of moving the compass farther away. The experiments show that as distance from the wire increases, the magnetic field gets weaker, so this change acts to decrease the deflection. Step 3: Combine the two effects. One change pushes the field stronger and the other pushes it weaker, so they oppose each other. Step 4: Conclusion. The qualitative rules tell us only the direction of each effect, not the precise amounts. Since the stronger-current effect and the greater-distance effect work against each other, we cannot say whether the field ends up stronger, weaker, or unchanged without knowing the exact numbers. The deflection therefore cannot be predicted with certainty from these rules alone.

questions.q_text: A straight vertical wire carries current flowing upward (from the floor toward the ceiling). Using the right-hand thumb rule, determine the direction of the magnetic field lines around the wire when viewed from above (looking down at the top of the wire).
questions.answer: Step 1: Identify the current direction. The current flows upward, so point your right thumb upward, toward the ceiling. Step 2: Curl your fingers around the wire. With the thumb pointing up, your fingers naturally curl around the wire. Step 3: View from above. When you look down from the top of the wire (with current coming toward you, out of the page), your curled fingers wrap in the counterclockwise (anticlockwise) direction. Conclusion: The magnetic field lines form circles that go counterclockwise around the wire as seen from above.

questions.q_text: A single loop carrying a certain current produces a magnetic field of strength B at its center. If you wind the same wire carrying the same current into a coil of 50 turns of the same radius, what is the field at the center, and explain why?
questions.answer: Step 1: Recall that the field from a current-carrying loop depends directly on the current. Step 2: In a coil, the current in each turn flows in the same direction, so each turn produces a field pointing the same way through the center. Step 3: Because the contributions add (reinforce), a coil with n turns gives a field n times that of one loop. Step 4: Here n = 50, so the field is 50 times B, that is 50B. The direction is straight through the coil, perpendicular to the plane of the turns.

questions.q_text: Explain why the magnetic field inside a solenoid is described as uniform, and state one practical advantage this gives.
questions.answer: Step 1: Look at the field lines inside a current-carrying solenoid. They are observed to be parallel, straight lines, all pointing in the same direction and evenly spaced apart. Step 2: When field lines are parallel, equally spaced, and in the same direction, it means the magnetic field has the same strength and the same direction at every point inside the coil. Step 3: A field that is identical at all points like this is by definition a uniform magnetic field — that is why the field inside the solenoid is called uniform. Step 4: Practical advantage — because the field is uniform, it is steady and predictable. This makes it very handy in applications, for example to magnetise a soft iron rod evenly to form a strong, controllable electromagnet.

questions.q_text: A horizontal aluminium rod hangs between the poles of a horse-shoe magnet, with the field pointing upward and current flowing through the rod. The rod jumps to the left. If you now reverse the current AND flip the magnet so the field points downward, which way will the rod jump? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: Start by noting the force direction depends on both the current direction and the field direction. Reversing just one of these two (the current OR the field) would reverse the direction of the force, making the rod jump to the right instead of left. But here we reverse BOTH the current and the field at the same time. Reversing the current flips the force once (left becomes right), and reversing the field flips it again (right becomes left). The two reversals cancel each other out. Therefore the rod jumps in the same direction as before — to the left.

questions.q_text: A house has its supply split into two circuits, one rated at 15 amperes and one rated at 5 amperes. Which circuit should a 2200 watt water geyser be connected to, and why? (The supply voltage is 220 volts.)
questions.answer: First, find the current the geyser draws. Current equals power divided by voltage. So current equals 2200 watts divided by 220 volts, which equals 10 amperes. Now compare this to the two circuits. The 5 ampere circuit cannot safely carry 10 amperes, because the current exceeds its rating and the fuse would blow. The 15 ampere circuit can carry 10 amperes safely since this is below its 15 ampere rating. Therefore the geyser should be connected to the 15 ampere circuit, which is meant for high-power appliances.
